rows: [p. 1] DIALOGUS PRIMUS. DE MATERIA MUNDI.
[p. 1] FIRST DIALOGUE. ON THE MATTER [MATERIA] OF THE WORLD.

[Margin: Nodus I. Introductio.] Meministi credo, optime Asphali (neque enim fas est oblitum te existimare, quae ipse a te accepta retineo) Meministi itaque narravisse te, quomodo cum Ereunio in tuo ad Rumi vada conducto, illaetam fallebas hyemem, cum interrumpit fortuitas ad focum fabulas vehementior ad fores pulsatio.

[Margin: Knot I. Introduction.] You remember, I believe, best Asphalius (for neither is it right [fas] to think you forgetful of the things which I myself retain, received from you) — you remember, therefore, that you narrated how, with Ereunius, in your [lodging] hired [conducto] at the shallows [vada] of Rumus [Rumi], you were beguiling [fallebas] the joyless winter, when a more vehement knocking at the doors interrupts the chance [fortuitas] tales at the hearth.

Neque internuncio opus fuit, irrupit enim ipsum interius conclave ubi sedebatis, Andabata, austro Poetarum penulam petasumque similis; et o vos Beatulos, inquit, Marina profecto numina, qui cavis his vestris abditi Vulcano facitis, et luctantes ventos tempestatesque sonoras securi contemnitis!

Nor was there need of a go-between [internuncio], for there burst into the very inner room [conclave] where you were sitting Andabata, like the South Wind [austro] of the Poets in cloak [penulam] and broad hat [petasum]; and 'O you little blessed ones [Beatulos],' he says, 'Marine deities [numina] surely, who, hidden in these hollows [cavis] of yours, sacrifice [facitis] to Vulcan, and, secure, despise the struggling winds and the resounding tempests!'
postquam autem assurrectum est et commutatae salutationes, et repositis [p. 2] humentibus illis velis in faciem suam rediit Andabata, oratus est ut eam noctem amicis, si non tempestati, commodaret.

But after there was a rising up [assurrectum est] and greetings were exchanged, and, those [p. 2] dripping coverings [velis] having been laid aside, Andabata returned into his own face, he was begged that he would grant [commodaret] that night to his friends, if not to the tempest.
Cum nihil impetraretur, tu clanculo Andabatae famulo insinuasti, ut equos quo tendebat Andabata, abduceret postridie reducturus: hanc esse Heri voluntatem.

When nothing was obtained, you secretly insinuated [insinuasti] to Andabata's servant that he should lead the horses away [to the place] whither Andabata was heading, being to bring [them] back on the next day: that this was the Master's [Heri] will.

Sic a tribus ad lucentem Vestam consessum est, protractaque confabulatio de infoelici apud nos actionis Christianae [Margin: Occasio sermonis.] statu, deque Reip. immutatione, quae prorsus imminere videbatur.

Thus by the three there was a sitting together [consessum est] at the shining Vesta, and a conversation [confabulatio] was drawn out about the unhappy [infoelici] state among us of Christian action [actionis Christianae] [Margin: The occasion of the conversation (sermonis).], and about the change [immutatione] of the Commonwealth [Reip.], which seemed altogether to impend.

Iamque noctem obrepsisse illata denunciabant lumina, cum surgens Andabata equos postulat, et utroque vestrum comitante in aream progressus, ut nitidam coeli faciem, spectabilemque Lunam, et micantia undique sydera est conspicatus, Quam inquit Deo rationem reddere possim noctem hanc apud vos desidens, cum ipse Deus tam illustri e sublimi illa pharo, itineris duce, tot accensis undique faculis ad viam provocet?

And now the lights brought in announced that night had crept on, when Andabata, rising, demands the horses, and, both of you accompanying, having gone forward into the courtyard [aream], when he caught sight of the shining face of the heaven, and the conspicuous [spectabilem] Moon, and the stars twinkling on every side, 'What account [rationem],' he says, 'could I render to God, sitting idle [desidens] this night with you, when God himself, from that so brilliant lofty lighthouse [pharo], the guide of the journey, with so many little torches [faculis] kindled on every side, calls [me] forth [provocet] to the road?'
Proh magnum numen, et pervigilem humani generis tutelam, a quo tot, et tam immensa corpora ad hoc unum creata sunt ut animalculo adeo despicabili, vel solatio vel miraculo forent!

'O great divinity [numen], and ever-watchful guardianship [tutelam] of the human race, by whom so many and so immense bodies have been created for this one [thing], that to a little animal [animalculo] so despicable they might be either for a solace or for a wonder [miraculo]!'
Hic Ereunius, Beatus es, inquit, Andabata qui horum corporum tam reconditos fines tam clare agnoscis, tam confidenter depraedicas.
Here Ereunius: 'Blessed are you,' he says, 'Andabata, who so clearly recognize, so confidently proclaim, the so hidden ends [fines] of these bodies.'

Et Andabata; illudis Ereuni, sed non me fallunt quae de influentiis a pluribus dicuntur. [p. 3] Verum ego haec in suspicionum genus magis quam opinionum reiicienda existimo. Et quoniam quae apud Philosophos non apparent, in non existentium classe collocantur, unus his corporibus scopus manet, ut hominum vel admirationi serviant, vel certe lucello alicui, ut cum Luna desit, horrorem tenebrarum dispescant umbris intermicantia;

And Andabata: 'You mock, Ereunius; but the things which are said by many [a pluribus] about influences [influentiis] do not escape me [non me fallunt]. [p. 3] But I think these are to be thrown back into the kind [genus] of suspicions rather than of opinions. And since the things which among the Philosophers do not appear are placed in the class of non-existents, one aim [scopus] remains for these bodies: that they should serve either the admiration [admirationi] of men, or certainly some little profit [lucello], that, when the Moon is lacking, twinkling among the shadows they may part asunder [dispescant] the horror of the darkness.'

Tum Ereunius, Ego vero, Andabata, noctem tibi hanc insomnem libens elargirer, ut vel hanc unam mihi veritatem certam redderes, teque a reddenda Deo ratione excusatum facerem, postquam meliori operae nequaquam indulgere te posse certo persuasus sum.

Then Ereunius: 'I indeed, Andabata, would gladly bestow [elargirer] on you this sleepless night, that you might render certain to me even this one truth; and I would make you excused from the account [ratione] to be rendered to God, since [postquam] I am certainly persuaded that you could by no means give yourself [indulgere] to a better work [operae].'

Cui Andabata, nisi iter urgeret et qui me hodie expectant sollicitos tenerem, tantam tibi evidentiam huius dicti pollicerer, ut ipse iurares reum esse violatae Christianae fidei quisquis oppositum sustinere audeat.

To whom Andabata: 'If the journey were not pressing, and [if] I were not holding anxious those who expect me today, I would promise you so great an evidence [evidentiam] of this saying, that you yourself would swear that whoever dares to maintain [sustinere] the opposite is guilty [reum] of violated Christian faith.'

Et suscipiens tu, si non aliud vetat, Andabata, hoc agamus, ego enim in me recipio neque quenquam te hac nocte expectare, neque iter te quoquam facturum. Iam pridem enim famulus te cras venturum nunciavit et equos tuos in stabula dimisit.

And you, taking [it] up: 'If nothing else forbids, Andabata, let us do this; for I take upon myself [in me recipio] [the assurance] that neither is anyone expecting you this night, nor will you make a journey anywhere. For long since the servant has announced that you will come tomorrow, and has dismissed your horses into the stables.'
Excanduit ad haec verba Andabata, sed illa ira, quam tua comitas et Ereunii mansuetudo facile lenirent. Sic in conclave reditum est, et mox illatus est secundarum mensarum mundus.

Andabata blazed up [excanduit] at these words, but with that anger which your courtesy and Ereunius' gentleness would easily soften. Thus there was a return into the room, and soon there was brought in the array [mundus] of the second tables [secundarum mensarum].

Ex pane frugibusque et herbis iuscula, fructus alii arefacti, [p. 4] conditi alii, cupediariorum inventa, et si quae alia per ieiunii legem permissa esculenta. Inciderat enim sextus post dominicam passioni sacer dies, quem hausta ab Aidano consuetudine, legeque ut ferunt a Dunstano indicta, religiosa Catholicae partis multitudo in Anglia abstemia celebrat.

Little broths [iuscula] out of bread and grains [frugibus] and herbs, fruits some dried, [p. 4] others preserved [conditi], the inventions of the confectioners [cupediariorum], and whatever other eatables [esculenta] [were] permitted through the law of fasting. For there had fallen [inciderat] the sixth day after the Lord's [day] [dominicam], sacred to the passion, which, by a custom drawn from Aidan, and by a law, as they say, proclaimed [indicta] by Dunstan, the religious multitude of the Catholic party [partis] in England celebrates abstinent [abstemia].

Remota mensa tu promissi commonefecisti Andabatam ad hos viros committendos nusquam piger, quorum Andabata eruditioni deditus vulgarisque Philosophiae peritus, quicquid scholis tritum erat, et corde, et fideli premebat memoria: sed negligentior horum Ereunius attentiorem ad ea oculum dirigebat quae ansulatim sibi connexa longo quasi reste trahit rationis necessitas.

The table having been removed, you reminded Andabata of [his] promise, being nowhere slow for matching [committendos] these men [against each other]; of whom Andabata, devoted to erudition and skilled in the common [vulgaris] Philosophy, whatever had been worn [tritum] in the schools, held it fast [premebat] both in heart and in faithful memory: but Ereunius, more negligent of these things, directed a more attentive eye to those things which the necessity of reason draws, connected to one another link by link [ansulatim], as if by a long rope.

Hic itaque parum authoritate movebatur, ille fidei gloria etiam in Philosophico pulvere ambiebat, et cum Platone errare sustinebat: cui veritatem Ereunius antehabebat, neque aliis quam oculis et evidentiae testibus fidebat.

This one [hic] therefore was little moved by authority; that one [ille] went canvassing [ambiebat] with the glory of faith even in the Philosophical dust, and bore [sustinebat] to err with Plato: to whom [cui] Ereunius preferred [antehabebat] truth, nor did he trust other witnesses than the eyes and evidence [evidentiae].

Tibi vero festus erat ille dies quo litem inter eos serere contingeret, ut tum contigit: quae quia implicatior accidit quam quae paucis cerni posset, eam sic repetere institui, ut vestra ipsorum nomina vicariam narrantis vim suppleant.

But to you that day was festive on which it fell out [contingeret] to sow a dispute [litem] between them, as then it fell out: which, because it happened more entangled [implicatior] than [one] which could be discerned in few [words], I have undertaken to repeat [repetere] it thus, that your own names may supply the vicarious force of the narrator.

[Margin: De fine Astrorum.] Andabata. Is sum ego qui hoc semper in Philosophia et Theologia Christiani hominis officium sum arbitratus, eas sententias mihi commendatas habere quae divinum hono-[p. 5]rem et pietatem in auditorum corda ingerant, ut ne tantum sapientiores sed et prudentiores exeant.

[Margin: On the end (fine) of the Stars.] Andabata. I am he who have always judged this [to be] the office [officium] of a Christian man in Philosophy and Theology: to have those opinions [sententias] commended to me which heap [ingerant] divine hon-[p. 5]our and piety into the hearts of the hearers, so that they may go out not only wiser but also more prudent.

Hoc ipso si quis principio non utatur, eum ego pronuncio impia iam rationis inire elementa, viamque indugredi sceleris: non Philosophiam, sed errorem sibi asciscere magistrum, et uno verbo scientiam illi non ad veritatem et vitam; sed ad superbiam et exitium valere.

If anyone does not use this very principle [principio], I pronounce that he is already entering upon impious elements of reason, and stepping into [indugredi] the way of wickedness: that he takes to himself [asciscere] as master not Philosophy but error, and, in one word, that science [scientiam] avails for him not toward truth and life, but toward pride and destruction.
Praeiacto hoc tam claro, tam forti, tam sancto fundamento, totum negotium brevi, sed efficacissima demonstratione concludo.
This so clear, so strong, so holy foundation having been laid beforehand [praeiacto], I conclude the whole business by a brief but most efficacious demonstration [demonstratione].

Cum enim nihil vel ad maiestatem Dei augustius, vel ad magnificentiam praeclarius, vel ad beneficentiam in humanum genus cumulatius dici possit, quam eum corpora tam vasta, tam multa, tam gloriosa ad tam leve humanae vitae commodum condidisse, palam asserendum est, indignum eum esse ut tam spectabili theatro fruatur qui conditoris ex eo gratiam non agnoscat. Habes sensum meum, Ereuni, contra quem quid moliaris expecto.

For since nothing can be said either more august toward the majesty of God, or more splendid toward [his] magnificence, or more heaped-up [cumulatius] toward [his] beneficence to the human race, than that he founded [condidisse] bodies so vast, so many, so glorious for so light a convenience [commodum] of human life, it is openly to be asserted that he is unworthy to enjoy so conspicuous [spectabili] a theatre who does not acknowledge from it the favour [gratiam] of the founder [conditoris]. You have my sense [sensum], Ereunius; against which I await what you may set in motion [moliaris].

Asphalius. Si cum tua gratia fiat, Ereuni, habeo quod opponam Andabatae, non de dicti veritate, neque enim in tuam messem falcem immittere ausim, sed de principio quod tanquam per se cognitum assumpsit, et de procedendi modo.

Asphalius. If it may be done with your leave [gratia], Ereunius, I have something to oppose to Andabata, not about the truth of the saying — for neither would I dare to send [my] sickle into your harvest — but about the principle [principio] which he has assumed as if known through itself [per se cognitum], and about the manner of proceeding.

Ereunius. Ego vero etiam gratiam referre paratus sum; non eo duntaxat nomine quod [p. 6] libentius aliena auscultem quam quicquam ex me proferam, sed ea praeterea ratione quod interea quid Andabatae respondeam, meditandi spatium adipiscar.

Ereunius. I indeed am ready even to return thanks [gratiam referre]; not on this account [nomine] only, that [p. 6] I more willingly listen to others' [things] than bring forth anything out of myself, but by this reason [ratione] besides, that meanwhile I may obtain space for meditating what I should answer to Andabata.
Asphalius. Agedum igitur, Andabata, hoc primum responde. Quomodo finem Astrorum accipis? num pro fructu et utilitate ex iis proveniente? et haec num aliud sonant quam effecta eorumdem?

Asphalius. Come on then, Andabata, answer this first. How do you take the end [finem] of the Stars? Is it as [pro] the fruit and utility coming forth from them? And do these [words] sound anything other than the effects [effecta] of the same?
Andab. Ut dicis.
Andab. As you say.

Asphal. Effecta vero qui comprehenderit, etiam caussam cognoscit; quare si omnes utilitates et adaequatum Astrorum finem cognoscis, eorumdem naturam compertam habes. Quod, quoniam te dicturum suspicari non possum, neque finem adaequatum te pernovisse arguo, neque negativam affirmare posse. i. ad aliud non esse instituta.

Asphal. But who has comprehended [comprehenderit] the effects, knows also the cause; wherefore if you know all the utilities and the adequate [adaequatum] end of the Stars, you have their nature found out [compertam]. Which, since I cannot suspect that you will say [it], I argue [arguo] that you neither have thoroughly known the adequate end, nor can affirm the negative, i.e. that they have not been instituted for anything else.

Andab. Ex parte recte ratiocinaris, sed meminisse oportet homines nos esse, et humanum esse ex iis quae nobis incidunt, argumentari: alia vero emolumenta syderum nulla nos contingunt: unde sola ista nos habere sollicitos debent.

Andab. In part you reason rightly; but it behoves [us] to remember that we are men, and that it is human to argue from those things which befall [incidunt] us: but no other emoluments of the stars reach [contingunt] us: whence these alone ought to hold us concerned [sollicitos].

Asphal. Amo te si propositae adhaereas regulae, sed negativa modo abstine, non enim nos vel per se vel per aliquod recte consequens afficit. Vide quoque num id non sequatur, peccare te in id quod maxima contentione profe-[p. 7]queris, et cum ad hoc aspires ut gloriam Deo accumules, dum id ipsum praeter naturam conaris, contrarium vel efficias vel efficere pericliteris.

Asphal. I love you if you adhere to the rule proposed; but only abstain from the negative, for it does not affect us either through itself or through anything rightly consequent. See also whether this does not follow: that you sin against [in] that which you pro-[p. 7]fess with the greatest exertion [contentione], and, while you aspire to this, that you may heap up glory for God, whilst you attempt that very thing beyond nature [praeter naturam], you either effect the contrary or run the risk [periclitere] of effecting [it].

Si enim quod Deus in re quaque instituit, ipsum procul dubio maxime ad honorem ipsius conducit, hoc autem an id sit quod amplexaris et defendendum suscipis, tu ignoras; sicubi contingat non esse, gloriae ipsius detrahis, et cum ubique incertus haereas, eo te perpetim obligas periculo. Crede itaque nimium anceps esse hoc fundamentum et ad perniciem aeque atque ad salutem ambiguum.

For if what God has instituted in each thing, that itself without doubt conduces most to his honour, but whether this is that which you embrace and undertake to be defended, you do not know; if anywhere it happens not to be [so], you detract from his glory, and since everywhere you stick [haereas] uncertain, you bind yourself continually [perpetim] to that danger. Believe therefore that this foundation is too two-edged [anceps], and ambiguous equally toward ruin as toward salvation [salutem].
Andab. Quid ergo? destituenda est Philosophia? relegandae in Insulas Mathematicas omnes scientiae et eae quidem quarum maxime arbitrio Res humana geritur?

Andab. What then? Is Philosophy to be abandoned? Are all the sciences to be banished [relegandae] into the Mathematical Islands, and those indeed by whose judgement [arbitrio] most of all the human Affair [Res humana] is carried on?

Asphal. Non ego quidem consulam, sed evocandarum ex iis angustiis scientiarum tibi Author sim. [Margin: Philosophiam non esse Logice tractandam.] An tu Metaphysicam vel naturalem vel moralem ullam scientiam extare censes, quando prolixis ultro citroque orationibus non Philosophicum sed Rhetoricum committitur certamen? Ubi post longas consumptas utrimque in dicendo horas, ad hoc tandem perventum est, ut incertum sit a qua parte veritas steterit et victoria?

Asphal. I indeed would not advise [it]; but I would be to you the Author of calling forth [evocandarum] the sciences out of those straits [angustiis]. [Margin: That Philosophy is not to be treated Logically.] Or do you think that any Metaphysical or natural or moral science exists [extare], when by prolix speeches to and fro [ultro citroque] not a Philosophical but a Rhetorical contest is engaged? Where, after long hours consumed on both sides in speaking, it is at last come to this, that it is uncertain on which side truth stood, and victory?

Age si quis te consulat in quovis negotio et tu ei respondeas; fortasse sic se res habet, fortassis autem plane contra, seu ut ille apud Poetam, quicquid di-[p. 8]co aut erit aut non; Divinare etenim Magnus mihi donat Apollo, non cum risu abeat consultor, et ad hoc consiliario se non indigere autumet?

Come, if anyone should consult you in any business whatever, and you should answer him: 'perhaps the matter holds itself so, but perhaps plainly the contrary'; or, as that [man] in the Poet: 'whatever I s-[p. 8]ay will either be or not; for great Apollo grants me to divine' — would not the consulter go away with a laugh, and declare [autumet] that for this he does not need a counsellor?
Nunc tuam conscientiam interrogo, postquam longis ambagibus in scientiis vestris ad probabilitatem, vel maiorem probabilitatem perventum est, quid amplius actum est?
Now I question your conscience: after, by long windings [ambagibus], in your sciences, it has been come to probability [probabilitatem], or greater probability, what more has been done?

Si enim quod probabile duntaxat est, falsum esse potest, etiam capax est ut maior ex adversa parte ostendatur veritatis species: si autem omni probabilitate alia maior esse potest, quod hodie magis probabile est, idem ipsum cras (si supervenerit ingeniosus oppositor) gradu illo cadet, cedetque oppositae propositioni.

For if what is only probable can be false, it is also capable [of this], that a greater appearance [species] of truth be shown from the opposite side: but if than every probability another can be greater, what today is more probable, that very same tomorrow (if an ingenious opponent shall have come upon [it]) will fall from that degree [gradu], and will yield to the opposite proposition.

Vides igitur tanto labore nihil plus effectum ad veritatem constituendam, quam si primo occursu Auditori responsum fuisset, forte sic habet, forte non: et a sortibus Antianis tam decisorium retulisset consultor oraculum quam a similibus Philisophiae [sic] Magistris.

You see therefore that by so great labour nothing more has been effected toward establishing truth, than if at the first encounter it had been answered to the Hearer, 'perchance it holds so, perchance not': and the consulter would have brought back an oracle as decisive from the Antian lots [sortibus Antianis] as from like Masters of Philosophy.

Eia igitur, Andabata, pro eo quo vales ingenio prima Philosophiae rudimenta constituere labora, et videbis quam sit facile ingens superstruere aedificium. Videbis umbras Philosophicas non minus laetas et patentes, quam sint hodie Mathematicae, velint modo homines et adlaborent. Verum interea ego gratiam Ereunii abutor, et exerceo patientiam.

Come then, Andabata, according to that wit [ingenio] in which you are strong, labour to establish the first rudiments of Philosophy, and you will see how easy it is to build upon [them] a huge edifice. You will see the Philosophical shades [umbras] no less glad [laetas] and open [patentes] than the Mathematical are today, if only men would be willing and labour at [it]. But meanwhile I abuse the favour [gratiam] of Ereunius, and exercise [his] patience.
Ereu. Imo Asphali, perge sis, quae enim di-[p. 9]cis cum nihil minus clara sint, tum longe ad vitam et actionem emendandam magis praeclara et proficua sunt quam quae ex me poteras expectare.

Ereu. Nay, Asphalius, go on, please [sis]; for the things which you s-[p. 9]ay, while [cum] they are in no way less clear, [so] also [tum] are they by far more splendid and more profitable for amending life and action than those which you could expect from me.

Andab. Imo tu, Ereuni, si quid habes, afferto: praeclara enim haec Asphalii monita inter febrientium somnia reponenda sunt, qui cum summa siti laborent, videntur sibi propter flumina aliamve potus copiam esse collocati, sed adeo Tantalica fortuna, ut semper aliquid minimi obicis a desiderato prohibeat latice: Sic Asphalius quod cupit, sic prope situm existimat, ut semper captet, nunquam apprehendat.

Andab. Nay, you, Ereunius, if you have anything, bring it forward: for these splendid admonitions of Asphalius are to be laid away [reponenda] among the dreams of the feverish, who, when they labour with the greatest thirst, seem to themselves to be placed beside [propter] rivers or some other abundance of drink, but with a fortune so Tantalean that always something of the smallest obstacle keeps [them] off from the desired liquid: so Asphalius thinks what he desires to be situated so near, that he always snatches at [captet] [it], never grasps [apprehendat] [it].

terms: vada = shallows, fords, or (poetically) the sea; Rumus is unidentified.
Probably an English coastal place Latinised, perhaps Romney (Kent), which suits the storm and the 'marine deities' joke. Not certain.
like the South Wind of the Poets
Auster, the stormy, rain-bringing south wind, which the poets picture dripping and cloaked (cf. Ovid, Met. 1.264–7).
Andabata comes in soaked from the storm.
cavis his vestris abditi … luctantes ventos tempestatesque sonoras
hidden in these hollows of yours … the struggling winds and the resounding tempests
Echoes Virgil, Aeneid 1.52–4 (Aeolus' cave: 'luctantes ventos tempestatesque sonoras'). The friends are cast as gods sheltering in a cave from the winds.
facere + dative = to make an offering to; also simply 'you serve the fire'.
A joke: they are sitting by the fire (Vulcan = fire).
His wet cloak and hat, compared to a ship's sails.
the practice or exercise of Christianity; 'the Christian cause'.
The friends talk of the bad state of (Catholic) Christianity in England and of a coming change of government. The book appeared in 1642, the year the English Civil War broke out.
Vesta = the hearth, the domestic fire (metonymy).
the Pharos of Alexandria; any beacon.
Andabata's name for the Moon, the 'guide of the journey'.
the astrological powers flowing from the stars to the earth.
This is the scholastic/astrological term. Andabata classes such claims as 'suspicions' (guesses), not real 'opinions'.
quae … non apparent, in non existentium classe collocantur
the things which do not appear are placed in the class of non-existents
Refers to the legal and scholastic maxim 'de non apparentibus et non existentibus eadem est ratio' (what does not appear is to be treated as what does not exist).
to separate, divide; here 'to break up, dispel'.
Probably a deliberate pun in a book De mundo: the 'world' of the dessert course. 'Secundae mensae' = the second course, i.e. dessert.
sextus post dominicam … dies, passioni sacer
the sixth day after the Lord's [day], sacred to the passion
Friday, the day of abstinence. White says the English custom of abstinence comes from St Aidan (d. 651) and that St Dunstan (d. 988) made it a law (with 'ut ferunt', 'as they say').
A rare adverb. The image is of propositions hooked together like links on a rope: demonstrative reasoning as opposed to authority.
vulgaris Philosophia; quicquid scholis tritum erat
the common Philosophy; whatever had been worn in the schools
The received scholastic, Aristotelian school philosophy, which Andabata stands for.

Cicero, Tusculans 1.39: 'errare mehercule malo cum Platone … quam cum istis vera sentire'. White adds the counter-maxim 'amicus Plato, magis amica veritas' through Ereunius, who 'held truth before' Plato.
went canvassing with the glory of faith
to go round, canvass, court, seek after.
Andabata courts the prestige of the faith even in philosophical disputes ('dust' = the arena or the geometer's sand).
the clearness or self-evidence of a thing to the mind or senses; not 'proof given'.
A key word for White: Ereunius trusts only 'the eyes and evidence'.
andabata = a gladiator who fought with his eyes covered (blindfold); Ereunius from Greek ἐρευνάω, 'to search out'; Asphalius from ἀσφάλεια, 'security, certainty'.
The names say who each speaker is: the blind fighter of the schools, the searcher, and the one who stands for certainty.
Aristotelian final cause. Asphalius identifies the 'end' (as use and fruit) with the 'effects'.
Scholastic: an 'adequate' end or object is one that exhausts the whole of what something is for.
Scholastic comprehensio, knowledge of a thing as fully as it is knowable. Whoever knows all of the effects knows the cause.
Scholastic term for a first principle that needs no proof.
to send [my] sickle into your harvest
A proverb, 'falcem in alienam messem mittere' (Erasmus, Adagia; cf. Deut. 23:25): to meddle in another's business.
gratia (cum tua gratia; gratiam referre; gratiam … abutor)
The speakers play on the word: Asphalius asks Ereunius' 'gratia' (leave), and Ereunius answers by 'returning gratia' (thanks).
Asphalius' point is logical: we cannot know that the stars serve no further end, so the negative claim cannot be affirmed.
contrary to, or outside, the nature of the thing.
Scholastic phrase: honouring God by claims that go against how things really are.
From relegatio in insulam, the Roman penalty of banishment to an island. Andabata asks whether only mathematics is to keep the name of science.
by the topical or dialectical logic of the schools, i.e. by probable arguments pro and contra.
This does not mean 'by reasoning'. White wants philosophy to be demonstrative like mathematics, not a debate of probabilities.
what is approvable or credible, backed by authority or opinion; not statistical.
The scholastic and Jesuit sense of 'probable opinion', which White attacks.
quicquid dico aut erit aut non; divinare etenim magnus mihi donat Apollo
whatever I say will either be or not; for great Apollo grants me to divine
Horace, Satires 2.5.59–60 (Tiresias to Ulysses). Quoted as a mock-oracle that says nothing.
The oracular lots of Fortuna at Antium (cf. Horace, Odes 1.35; Macrobius, Sat. 1.23.13).
shades = shady walks or groves where philosophy is taught (umbra = the leisured school); also 'shadows'.
The image is of the Academy's groves. Asphalius wants philosophy's 'shades' to be as fruitful and open as mathematics.
Tantalus, who stood in water he could never drink (Homer, Od. 11.582–92; Ovid, Met. 4.458–9).
near, close by (the old local sense); not 'on account of'.
In this phrase propter has its archaic local meaning.
notes: Unit: Dialogue I, Knot i, PDF pp. 12–20 = printed pp. 1–9. It ends at Andabata's speech closing '…nunquam apprehendat' on p. 9. Knot ii ('Mundum non esse infinitum') starts on the same page with Ereunius' 'Quoniam utrique sedit eadem voluntas', where the margin has 'Nodus II. Mundum non esse infinitum'. The page offset of +11 holds throughout (p. 9 = PDF 20).

The table of Knots gives 'Occasio sermonis' at p. 2. In the text the margin 'Nodus I. Introductio' stands at the opening on p. 1, and the gloss 'Occasio sermonis' is on p. 2 next to the line 'statu, deque Reip. immutatione'. A second gloss, 'De fine Astrorum', is on p. 4 and a third, 'Philosophiam non esse Logice tractandam', on p. 7. All are given in place as [Margin: …].

Rows: the opening narrative (pp. 1–4) is printed as a single paragraph. It is split here into rows at sentence breaks so the Latin and English line up. Speeches have one row each, and long speeches are split at sentence breaks. Printed page breaks are marked [p. n] in both columns (with the word-split shown as 'hono-[p. 5]rem' etc.).

Conventions (as in glossary.md): long s → s; æ/œ → ae/oe; ę → ae; tildes expanded (probabilitatē → probabilitatem, ipsū → ipsum, nō → non, primū → primum); consonantal u → v (vestris, Vulcano); i kept; accents dropped (à, cùm, verò). 'Reip.' is kept as printed. 'Ereunij/Asphalij' → Ereunii/Asphalii. 'pergesis' is printed as one word and is given here as 'perge sis' (= si vis, 'please').

Printed oddities kept: 'Philisophiae' (p. 8, a misprint for Philosophiae) marked [sic]; 'infoelici', 'sydera', 'caussam', 'authoritate', 'Author' kept as spelled. 'abutor' takes an accusative ('gratiam … abutor'), which is post-classical but is kept.

Uncertain: 'Rumi vada' — the place is not identified (perhaps Romney). 'quo tendebat Andabata' is read as 'to where Andabata was heading'. In the morning, as the servant later reports, he has gone on to announce Andabata's arrival 'tomorrow' and has put the horses in the stables. 'hic … ille' (p. 4) is read in the usual way: hic = Ereunius (the latter named), ille = Andabata. This fits the sense: Ereunius is 'little moved by authority', and Andabata 'bore to err with Plato'. 'cui' = Plato.

Verification pass: the transcription was compared again with the page images, and the English with the Latin, sentence by sentence (cases, tenses, moods, negatives, comparatives, omissions). This gave 4 corrections: (1) transcription p. 7: 'periclitere' → 'pericliteris', as printed; (2) 'a pluribus' had been over-translated as 'by very many' and is now 'by many'; (3) 'num pro fructu': 'Is it for the fruit' → 'Is it as [pro] the fruit', since pro = 'as, in place of'; (4) 'cui veritatem Ereunius antehabebat': 'before whom … held truth' → 'to whom … preferred truth', keeping the dative construction. No omissions or additions were found. Still uncertain: the identity of 'Rumi vada' and the exact sense of 'quo tendebat' (see above). The margin 'Philosophiam non esse Logice tractandam' is read as 'not by dialectical/probable disputation'.
